pull_requests.title: fix: session.verify=False should take precedence over REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE
pull_requests.body:
Fixes #3829

**Problem:** When `session.verify = False` is explicitly set, calling `session.get(url)` (without passing verify) still picks up `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` from the environment, causing SSL verification to fail with a self-signed or untrusted cert.

**Root cause:** In `merge_environment_settings()`, when `verify` parameter is `None` (not passed by caller), the environment variable lookup runs unconditionally and sets verify to the CA bundle path. Then `merge_setting(env_path, self.verify=False)` returns the env path because neither arg is None — request_setting takes priority over session_setting for non-dict values.

**Fix:** Skip the environment CA bundle lookup when `self.verify is False`. This preserves the user's explicit intent to disable verification, while keeping the existing behavior for all other cases (default sessions, explicit `verify=True`, etc.).

**Behavior after fix:**
- `session.verify = False; session.get(url)` → verify stays `False` ✅
- Default session with REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE set → uses env bundle ✅ (unchanged)
- Explicit `verify=True` in request → uses env bundle ✅ (unchanged)
- Explicit `verify=False` in request → `False` ✅ (unchanged)

pull_requests.title: fix: handle bytes username/password in HTTPDigestAuth
pull_requests.body:
## Summary

When `username` or `password` is passed as bytes to `HTTPDigestAuth` (e.g. users following the workaround for non-ASCII credentials from issue #5089), `build_digest_header` would include the bytes repr (`b'...'`) in the Authorization header value, producing an invalid header like:

```
Digest username="b'Ond\xc5\x99ej'", realm="..."
```

## Fix

Decode bytes to UTF-8 strings at the start of `build_digest_header`, before they are used in both hash computation (A1 string) and header formatting. This matches the pattern already used by the inner hash functions (`md5_utf8`, etc.) which accept both str and bytes.

Fixes #6102

pull_requests.title: fix: reject None values in auth tuple
pull_requests.body:
When `auth` is a 2-tuple containing `None` values, `prepare_auth` passes it to `HTTPBasicAuth` because `(None, None)` is truthy. This sends `"None:None"` as Basic Auth credentials instead of being rejected.

```python
from requests.models import PreparedRequest
pr = PreparedRequest()
pr.prepare(method="GET", url="http://example.com/", auth=(None, None))
# Sends: Authorization: Basic Tm9uZTpOb25l (decodes to "None:None")
```

Raised `InvalidHeader` when either username or password is `None`, so the error is caught at preparation time rather than silently sending garbage credentials.

pull_requests.title: fix: handle non-ASCII (Unicode) credentials in HTTPDigestAuth
pull_requests.body:
## Problem

`HTTPDigestAuth` mishandles non-ASCII usernames and passwords in two ways:

**1. Unicode str → invalid HTTP header**
```python
HTTPDigestAuth('Ondřej', 'heslíčko')
# produces: Digest username="Ondřej", ...
# → non-ASCII bytes in a header field; invalid per HTTP spec
```

**2. Pre-encoded bytes → bytes repr in header**
The previously suggested workaround of passing pre-encoded bytes produces:
```python
HTTPDigestAuth('Ondřej'.encode('utf-8'), 'heslíčko')
# produces: Digest username="b'Ond\xc5\x99ej'", ...
# → Python bytes repr embedded in header; completely wrong
```

Closes #6102

## Solution

Two targeted changes to `build_digest_header`:

### 1. Normalize bytes → str early
```python
if isinstance(username, bytes):
    username = username.decode("utf-8")
if isinstance(password, bytes):
    password = password.decode("utf-8")
```
This ensures both the hash computation and header construction always work with `str`.

### 2. RFC 5987 encoding for non-ASCII usernames
Per [RFC 7616 §3.4](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7616#section-3.4), when a username cannot be represented as a quoted ASCII string, the `username*` parameter with RFC 5987 encoding must be used:

```python
try:
    username.encode("ascii")
    username_field = f'username="{username}"'
except UnicodeEncodeError:
    username_field = f"username*=UTF-8''{urlquote(username, safe='')}"
```

ASCII usernames produce the same output as before. Non-ASCII usernames produce:
```
Digest username*=UTF-8''Ond%C5%99ej, realm="...", ...
```

The hash computation (`A1 = username:realm:password`) already uses UTF-8 encoding via `hash_utf8`, which is correct per RFC 7616 §6.1.

pull_requests.body:
Closes #6653

## Summary

Adds `:raises:` RST docstring entries to the `request()` function documenting the exceptions that callers should be prepared to handle.

The documentation is added only on the main `request()` function (not repeated on each convenience method like `get()`, `post()`, etc.) to avoid duplication — all convenience methods delegate to `request()` and can raise the same exceptions.

## Exceptions documented

| Exception | When raised |
|-----------|-------------|
| `ConnectionError` | Network problem (DNS failure, refused connection, etc.) |
| `Timeout` | Request timed out (wraps `ConnectTimeout` and `ReadTimeout`) |
| `TooManyRedirects` | Configured redirect limit exceeded |
| `URLRequired` | No URL provided |
| `MissingSchema` | URL has no scheme (e.g. missing `http://`) |
| `InvalidSchema` | URL scheme is invalid or unsupported |
| `InvalidURL` | URL is otherwise malformed |
| `InvalidHeader` | A header value is invalid |

These match the exceptions listed in the [Requests exceptions API docs](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/#exceptions) that are relevant to the request() call itself (as opposed to exceptions from response processing like `JSONDecodeError`).

pull_requests.title: Fix infinite redirect loop with FQDN trailing dot
pull_requests.body:
## Problem

When making a request to a URL with a trailing dot FQDN (e.g. `https://pyropus.ca./`), `requests` gets stuck in an infinite redirect loop, eventually raising `TooManyRedirects`.

The server redirects to the non-FQDN version (`https://pyropus.ca/`), but the FQDN trailing dot in the Host header causes requests to see the same URL and loops infinitely.

 Browsers and curl normalize FQDNs by stripping the trailing dot.

## Fix

Strip trailing dot from host during URL preparation in `prepare_url()`. This ensures the Host header is sent without the trailing dot, preventing the redirect loop.
 Also fix overly strict validation that rejected all hosts starting with `.` - only leading dots should be rejected ( not bare dots at the start of a label).
 Add a comment explaining the RFC 1035 context.
## Testing

Before:
```python
requests.get("https://pyropus.ca./")  # TooManyRedirects
```
After
```python
requests.get("https://pyropus.ca./")  # 200 OK
```

Closes #7209

pull_requests.title: Fix #7122: Preserve cookie policy in prepare_request
pull_requests.body:
Fixes #7122

## Problem
When a custom `CookiePolicy` is set on a Session's cookie jar, it is ignored when preparing requests. This was previously reported in #3416 and fixed in #4042, but that fix was merged into an abandoned `proposed/3.0.0` branch.

## Root Cause
In `prepare_request()`, the session cookies are merged using:
```python
merged_cookies = merge_cookies(
    merge_cookies(RequestsCookieJar(), self.cookies), cookies
)
```
This creates a new `RequestsCookieJar` without the original policy.

## Solution
Based on the fix from #4042:

1. Added `_copy_cookie_jar()` function in `cookies.py` to copy a CookieJar while preserving its policy
2. Modified `RequestsCookieJar.copy()` to pass `self._policy` to the new instance
3. Modified `prepare_request()` in `sessions.py` to use `_copy_cookie_jar()` instead of creating a new jar

## Changes
- `src/requests/cookies.py`: Added `_copy_cookie_jar()` and fixed `copy()` method
- `src/requests/sessions.py`: Use `_copy_cookie_jar()` to preserve policy

## Testing
Users can now set custom cookie policies that will be respected:
```python
import cookielib
import requests

class MyPolicy(cookielib.DefaultCookiePolicy):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(blocked_domains=['example.com'])

s = requests.Session()
s.cookies.set_policy(MyPolicy())
# Policy will now be preserved across requests
```

---
*This PR revives the fix from #4042 for the current codebase.*

## Summary

This change fixes `Response.iter_lines()` when it is called repeatedly on the
same streaming response.

```python
import requests

r = requests.get("https://httpbin.org/stream/4", stream=True)

next(r.iter_lines())
remaining = list(r.iter_lines())

pull_requests.title: Move DigestAuth hash algorithms to use usedforsecurity=False
pull_requests.body:
This PR moves the DigestAuth hash algorithms to use `usedforsecurity=False`. This is to both avoid unnecessarily breaking DigestAuth on FIPS enabled systems and to make it clearer to security reporters these are not a security control.

[RFC 7616](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7616) makes it clear algorithm choice is decided by the server being called and the choice for hashing algorithm does not meaningfully change the risk profile for Digest auth usage.

> HTTP Digest Authentication, when used with human-memorable passwords,
   is vulnerable to dictionary attacks.  Such attacks are much easier
   than cryptographic attacks on any widely used algorithm, including
   those that are no longer considered secure.  **In other words,
   algorithm agility does not make this usage any more secure.**
   
\- [RFC 7616 § 5.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7616#section-5.1)

pull_requests.title: Fix NO_PROXY domain suffix matching (enforce label boundary)
pull_requests.body:
### Description

This PR fixes incorrect domain suffix matching behavior in `should_bypass_proxies()`.

Previously, `NO_PROXY` entries were matched using a raw string `.endswith()` check. This allowed unintended matches where a hostname merely ended with the same string but was not a true subdomain.

For example:

```text
NO_PROXY=example.com
request → attackerexample.com
```

This incorrectly matched and caused the request to bypass the configured proxy.

---

### Fix

The matching logic has been updated to enforce proper domain boundaries:

* A hostname must either:

  * exactly match the `NO_PROXY` entry, or
  * be a subdomain (i.e., end with `"." + candidate`)

This ensures only valid domain relationships are considered.

---

### Additional Improvement

Trailing-dot Fully Qualified Domain Names (FQDNs), such as `internal.corp.`, are now normalized before comparison using:

```python
hostname = hostname.rstrip(".")
```

This aligns hostname comparison with standard DNS semantics and avoids mismatches due to formatting differences.

---

### Motivation

This change ensures that `NO_PROXY` behavior is consistent and avoids incorrect proxy routing caused by naive suffix matching.

---

### Testing

* Added test cases covering:

  * exact matches (`example.com`)
  * subdomains (`sub.example.com`)
  * non-matching lookalike domains (`attackerexample.com`)
  * trailing-dot normalization (`example.com.`)

* Verified behavior remains unchanged for valid existing cases.

pull_requests.title: fix: decode bytes credentials in HTTPDigestAuth (fixes #6102)
pull_requests.body:
## Problem

When bytes are passed as `username` or `password` to `HTTPDigestAuth` (a common pattern for non-latin credentials like Cyrillic), the f-string in `build_digest_header` formats them as `b'...'` instead of the actual string value:

```python
# User code:
auth = requests.auth.HTTPDigestAuth("Сергей".encode("utf-8"), "pwd")
# Result: A1 = "b'\\xd0\\xa1...'" instead of "Сергей:realm:pwd"
```

This produces a wrong MD5/SHA hash and an invalid `Authorization` header.

## Fix

Decode `bytes` credentials to `str` (UTF-8) before building the A1 string and the Authorization header value:

```python
username = (
    self.username.decode("utf-8")
    if isinstance(self.username, bytes) else self.username
)
```

Applies to both `username` (A1 + Authorization header) and `password` (A1).

**1 new test. 238 upstream tests pass — 0 regressions.** Fixes #6102.

pull_requests.title: Fix HTTPDigestAuth bytes handling for non-latin credentials (#6102)
pull_requests.body:
## Problem

When `username` or `password` are passed as `bytes` to `HTTPDigestAuth`, they are directly interpolated into f-strings in `build_digest_header()`, producing their `repr()` (e.g., `b'Ond\\xc5\\x99ej'`) instead of the decoded string value.

This causes Digest auth to send malformed headers like `username="b'Ond\\xc5\\x99ej'"` when users encode non-latin credentials as UTF-8 bytes.

**Reproduction:**
```python
import requests
auth = requests.auth.HTTPDigestAuth('Ondřej'.encode('utf-8'), 'heslíčko')
# The generated header incorrectly contains username="b'Ond\\xc5\\x99ej'"
```

## Fix

Decode `bytes` to `str` (UTF-8) in `HTTPDigestAuth.__init__()`, consistent with how `_basic_auth_str` handles bytes input.

## Changes

- `src/requests/auth.py`: Add bytes-to-str decoding in `HTTPDigestAuth.__init__()` (4 lines added)

Fixes #6102

pull_requests.title: Fix HTTPDigestAuth bytes representation in Authorization header
pull_requests.body:
## Problem

When users pass UTF-8 encoded bytes to `HTTPDigestAuth` (as previously recommended in issue #5089), the Authorization header displays the Python bytes representation instead of the actual username:

```python
HTTPDigestAuth('Ondřej'.encode('utf-8'), 'heslíčko')
# Creates header: Digest username="b'Ond\\xc5\\x99ej'"  ❌
# Should be:        Digest username="Ondřej"            ✓
```

This happens because f-string formatting converts bytes objects to their `repr()` representation (e.g., `b'Ond\xc5\x99ej'`), corrupting the credentials in the HTTP header.

## Root Cause

The code was using `self.username` and `self.password` directly in f-strings without checking their type. When bytes are passed, Python's string interpolation produces the literal bytes representation rather than the decoded characters.

## Solution

Decode bytes credentials back to UTF-8 strings before using them in string formatting:

```python
# Ensure username and password are strings, not bytes
username = self.username
password = self.password
if isinstance(username, bytes):
    username = username.decode("utf-8")
if isinstance(password, bytes):
    password = password.decode("utf-8")
```

This fix:
1. **Accepts both strings and bytes** - backward compatible with existing code
2. **Decodes to UTF-8** - per RFC 7616 requirements for Digest authentication
3. **Fails fast on invalid UTF-8** - strict decoding alerts users to malformed input
4. **Uses decoded values in f-strings** - prevents bytes repr from appearing in headers

## Verification

Tested with non-latin credentials:
```python
auth = HTTPDigestAuth('Ondřej'.encode('utf-8'), 'heslíčko')
# Authorization header now correctly shows: username="Ondřej"
```

Also verified that plain string credentials continue to work:
```python
auth = HTTPDigestAuth('Ondřej', 'heslíčko')  # Still works ✓
```

## Limitations

- This fix handles UTF-8 encoded bytes, but if users pass other encodings (e.g., Latin-1), decoding will fail. This is intentional—RFC 7616 specifies UTF-8, and failing fast is safer than silently corrupting credentials.
- The actual UTF-8 encoding still happens later in `hash_utf8()`, which is the correct place per the Digest auth specification.

## Related Issues

Closes #5089 (the original bug report with incorrect workaround)

pull_requests.title: Add inline types to Requests
pull_requests.body:
# Add inline type annotations

> [!IMPORTANT]
> We want feedback from people who actively maintain projects that depend on Requests or use it heavily. Please share your experience testing this against your code **in the linked issue**.
>
>Comments that are clearly AI-generated will be hidden or removed. This is a library written "for Humans". The conversation is between maintainers and users, not a prompt.

## Overview

This PR adds type annotations throughout Requests to codify the type contract alongside the code. This is a path for what inline typing in Requests _could_ look like. The goals are to establish what APIs are intended to support, make more reasoned decisions about code changes, and make using Requests in a modern development environment easier.

The package passes strict type checking with pyright, with the caveat that a few decisions on internals have been deferred for discussion by the maintainers and broader community. Right now, the intended behavior for those is undefined.

Related issue: [RFC: Adding inline type annotations to Requests](https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/7271)
Currently tracked TODOs: https://gist.github.com/nateprewitt/3e65fc8c3e9db3d5629ec1daf1f993f8

## How to verify locally

```
pip install pyright typing-extensions
python -m pyright src/requests/
```

Should report 0 errors. `typing-extensions` is needed on Python 3.10-3.12.

## Main design decisions

- `cast()` over `assert/isinstance` for type narrowing to avoid breaking downstream code at runtime
- New `_types.py` module centralizing Protocols, type aliases, and TypeVars
- `SupportsRead`/`SupportsItems` as `@runtime_checkable` Protocols replacing `hasattr` checks
- `is_prepared()` as a `TypeIs` guard that's a no-op at runtime (always returns `True`)
- ~100 type suppressions, each documented with an inline PR comment

## Runtime impact

A full catalog of every runtime-impacting change is available [here](https://gist.github.com/nateprewitt/08a622a4bd8895a9c4a7a7047b088648). The behavioral changes and bug fixes are the ones worth scrutinizing. The rest is mechanical.

## Open discussion points

- **`str` vs `bytes` URL handling**: Requests has historically accepted both when Python 2.7 was primary usage. These types currently declare `str` only. This needs a decision on whether to fix existing broken bytes behavior or formalize the `str`-only contract.
- **`yield_requests` API**: Needs documentation and a decision on how this should even work in practice. This API decision came through without review and I don't think there's any realistic usage outside of the library.

## What's NOT in this PR

- **mypy compatibility**: Developed against pyright. If we do add mypy, that will be in a separate follow-up. Public API types should still work for mypy users.
- **Public API changes**: No signature changes, no new exceptions, no runtime assertions.
- **Test type-checking**: Tests are not under strict mode. There are a number of tests that intentionally violate the type contract. We'll address those once we have a final plan here.

pull_requests.title: Fix HTTPDigestAuth header corruption when credentials are bytes
pull_requests.body:
Fixes #6102.

## Problem

When `HTTPDigestAuth` is constructed with bytes credentials (the workaround suggested in the issue thread), the `build_digest_header` method interpolates them directly into f-strings. Python formats a bytes object as its repr, so `'Ondřej'.encode('utf-8')` becomes `b'Ond\xc5\x99ej'` in the header:

```
Digest username="b'Ond\xc5\x99ej'"
```

This is wrong in two ways: the `b''` wrapper appears literally, and non-ASCII bytes are shown as escape sequences rather than the actual character.

## Fix

Decode bytes `username` and `password` to str via UTF-8 at the top of `build_digest_header`, before they are used in the A1 hash computation or the header string. This is consistent with how the internal hash functions already handle encoding (they encode str to UTF-8 bytes for hashing).

## Behaviour after fix

```python
# bytes credentials produce a correct header
auth = HTTPDigestAuth('Ondřej'.encode('utf-8'), 'heslíčko'.encode('utf-8'))
# header now contains: username="Ondřej"

# str credentials are unchanged
auth = HTTPDigestAuth('user', 'pass')
# header now contains: username="user"
```

All existing tests pass.

pull_requests.title: Fix case-insensitive header lookup in get_encoding_from_headers
pull_requests.body:
The `get_encoding_from_headers` function uses `headers.get("content-type")` which is case-sensitive. When a plain Python dict is passed with the key `"Content-Type"`, the lookup returns `None` and the function exits early — never reaching the charset parsing logic.

This causes the function to incorrectly return `None` even when a valid charset is present in the header.

Fix: Wrap the headers dict in `CaseInsensitiveDict` before lookup, so both `"content-type"` and `"Content-Type"` (and any other casing) are handled correctly.

Fixes #7234

pull_requests.body:
## Summary
Enable automatic content decoding on `Response.raw` so streamed gzip-encoded responses can be consumed directly via file-like readers.

## Root Cause
Requests built responses with `raw.decode_content=False`, so consumers reading from `response.raw` got compressed bytes by default. This breaks file-like streaming parsers that call `.read()` and expect decoded content.

## Changes Made
- Set `response.raw.decode_content = True` in `HTTPAdapter.build_response`.
- Added a regression test in `tests/test_adapters.py` to verify `build_response` enables decoded raw reads by default.

## Verification
- Ran: `PYTHONPATH=src pytest -q tests/test_adapters.py`
- Result: `2 passed`

## Notes
- Explicit reads that need wire-level compressed bytes can still request `decode_content=False` on read/stream calls.


Closes #2155

pull_requests.title: Fix RequestsCookieJar MutableMapping mismatch
pull_requests.body:
## Summary

`RequestsCookieJar` currently inherits from both `CookieJar` and
`MutableMapping`, but it does not actually satisfy the `MutableMapping`
contract.

`CookieJar.__iter__` yields `Cookie` objects, while `MutableMapping` expects
iteration over keys. That means `RequestsCookieJar` can report itself as a
`MutableMapping` even though code written against that interface will fail.

This change removes the `MutableMapping` base class from
`RequestsCookieJar` while keeping its existing dict-like convenience methods.

## What changed

- removed `MutableMapping` from `RequestsCookieJar`'s base classes
- kept the existing dict-like API (`get`, `set`, `keys`, `items`, etc.)
- added explicit implementations for behavior that had been inherited from
  `MutableMapping`:
  - `__contains__`
  - `update`
  - `__eq__`
- added a regression test to verify `RequestsCookieJar` is no longer treated
  as a `MutableMapping`

## Why this approach

I considered changing iteration to yield keys instead, but that would also
change the current behavior of iterating over a cookie jar, which today yields
`Cookie` objects.

Removing the incorrect ABC inheritance seemed safer than changing iteration
semantics.

## Testing

Ran a focused local test slice covering the changed behavior:

- `tests/test_requests.py -k 'prepared_copy or cookie_jar_is_not_a_mutable_mapping or cookie_as_dict or cookie_parameters or cookie_duplicate_names'`

Result:
- 13 passed

I also compared a full local test run on a clean clone versus this branch.

Clean clone:
- 400 passed
- 15 skipped
- 1 xfailed
- 196 errors

Patched branch:
- 401 passed
- 15 skipped
- 1 xfailed
- 196 errors

The extra passing test is the new regression test. The 196 errors were already
present on a clean clone in my environment.

Closes #7228

pull_requests.title: Fix: Replace fragile assert with explicit TypeError in _internal_utils.py
pull_requests.body:
### Summary
The [unicode_is_ascii](cci:1://file:///c:/Users/lahya/Desktop/pyspectre_release/pysymex_v0.1.0%20alpha/pysymex_release/requests/src/requests/_internal_utils.py:38:0-53:20) function in [_internal_utils.py](cci:7://file:///c:/Users/lahya/Desktop/pyspectre_release/pysymex_v0.1.0%20alpha/pysymex_release/requests/src/requests/_internal_utils.py:0:0-0:0) currently relies on an `assert isinstance(u_string, str)` statement to guard the `.encode("ascii")` method call. 

While this prevents invalid inputs in standard environments, [assert](cci:1://file:///c:/Users/lahya/Desktop/pyspectre_release/pysymex_v0.1.0%20alpha/pysymex_release/benchmark_extreme.py:286:0-290:16) statements are completely stripped from the Python bytecode when execution runs with the `-O` optimization flag. 

If an optimized production environment inadvertently passes a non-string object here, the assert is bypassed and execution falls through to `.encode("ascii")`, causing an uncaught `AttributeError` which hides the root type failure. 

### What this PR does
This PR replaces the fragile [assert](cci:1://file:///c:/Users/lahya/Desktop/pyspectre_release/pysymex_v0.1.0%20alpha/pysymex_release/benchmark_extreme.py:286:0-290:16) with an explicit `if not isinstance(u_string, str): raise TypeError(...)` structural pattern. This guarantees that malformed arguments are caught elegantly regardless of execution environment or optimization flags, making the internal API fundamentally more robust and debuggable.

- clarify in `docs/user/advanced.rst` that `requests.certs.where()` / `DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH` are not necessarily the effective CA bundle for a specific request
- document that the effective CA bundle can come from per-request `verify`, `Session.verify`, or `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` / `CURL_CA_BUNDLE`

This aims to cover the broader confusion from #6565 (not only the function docstring).

Fixes #6565

issues.title: TestTimeout abandons three delay/10 requests and later tests wait out the server
issues.body:
`TestTimeout` makes three requests to `httpbin("delay/10")` and abandons all of them:

- `tests/test_requests.py:2539`, `test_stream_timeout`, `timeout=2.0`
- `tests/test_requests.py:2573`, `test_read_timeout`, parametrized, `timeout=0.1` (two params)

The client raises at 2.0s and 0.1s, but the pytest-httpbin server keeps sleeping the full 10 seconds and serves requests serially. The next test that needs the server blocks until those sleeps finish.

```
$ pytest "tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_encoded_methods" -p no:randomly
1 passed in 0.56s

$ pytest "tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_read_timeout" \
         "tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_encoded_methods" \
         -p no:randomly --durations=5
19.79s call     tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_encoded_methods
 0.11s call     tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_read_timeout[timeout1]
 0.10s call     tests/test_requests.py::TestTimeout::test_read_timeout[timeout0]
3 passed in 20.55s
```

`test_encoded_methods` is one line (`requests.request(b"GET", httpbin("get"))`). The 19.79s is 2 x 10s of server sleep minus the 0.2s the two clients used. In a full run the cost lands on whichever tests happen to follow:

```
19.35s call     TestTimeout::test_encoded_methods
 8.00s call     TestTimeout::test_none_timeout[None]
```

Both call sites need the server to outlast the client timeout, not to sleep for 10 seconds. Lowering the delays leaves the assertions unchanged:

- line 2539, `delay/10` to `delay/3` (client timeout 2.0)
- line 2573, `delay/10` to `delay/1` (client timeout 0.1)

With that change, `TestTimeout` goes from 30.56s to 5.70s and the full suite from 167.44s to 142.04s, with the same results either way: 630 passed, 3 skipped, 1 xpassed. The single failure in both runs is `TestPreparingURLs::test_different_connection_pool_for_tls_settings_verify_bundle_unexpired_cert`, which is unrelated and fails before the change as well.

Measured at 611c616 on Windows 11, Python 3.14.2, pytest 9.1.1.

issues.title: proxy_bypass_registry uses unanchored re.match (Windows proxy bypass)
issues.body:
This was discussed here multiple times in the past so I'm opening it as a public bug report.

`src/requests/utils.py`, `proxy_bypass_registry` (main, 2.34.2):

```python
if re.match(test, host, re.I):   # start-anchored only
    return True
```

re.match anchors only the start, so ProxyOverride=google.com matches google.com.evil.com and bypasses the proxy for it — an attacker-influenced hostname can escape a proxy meant to inspect traffic.

Diverges from CPython: this is a copy of CPython's old code. CPython now matches with fnmatch (anchored both ends, wildcards preserved). Verified on 3.14:
- `fnmatch("google.com.evil.com", "google.com")` → False (requests returns True)
- `fnmatch("a.example.net", "*.example.net")` → True

Fix: use fnmatch(host, test) to match CPython, or minimally anchor: re.match(test + r"\Z", host, re.I).

issues.title: Docstring examples in `from_key_val_list` show the pre-3.12 OrderedDict repr
issues.body:
`src/requests/utils.py`'s `from_key_val_list` docstring shows:

    >>> from_key_val_list([('key', 'val')])
    OrderedDict([('key', 'val')])

Since Python 3.12, `collections.OrderedDict.__repr__` uses the regular dict form ([cpython gh-101446](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/101446)), so on any currently supported Python this actually prints:

    OrderedDict({'key': 'val'})

Reproducer (Python 3.13.5, requests 2.34.2):

```
>>> from requests.utils import from_key_val_list
>>> from_key_val_list([('key', 'val')])
OrderedDict({'key': 'val'})
>>> from_key_val_list({'key': 'val'})
OrderedDict({'key': 'val'})
```

The `ValueError` example in the same docstring is still accurate. Both stale occurrences are on lines 351 and 357, and a grep of the rest of the package found no others.

I have a two-line fix ready on a fork and would be glad to open a pull request if that's welcome. (The compare page says PRs are limited to collaborators, hence this issue.)

issues.title: API-provided proxies are silently overridden by environment variables; no per-request opt-out

labels.name: actions/autoclose-feat
labels.description: Used for automation to auto-close an issue

issues.body:
Summary
Requests automatically uses environment proxies from HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, etc. There is currently no clean per-request way to disable this behavior. The only reliable workaround is to create a Session and set ```session.trust_env = False.```

Current behavior
When proxy-related environment variables are present, a simple request such as:
```
requests.get(url, proxies={})
```
still uses the environment proxy. Passing an empty proxies dict does not mean “disable all proxies”; it means “no API-level proxy was provided”, so environment proxies are merged in by Session.merge_environment_settings() when trust_env is True.

To actually bypass environment proxies, users must write:

```
session = requests.Session()
session.trust_env = False
session.get(url)
```
They cannot write:

```
requests.get(url, trust_env=False)
```
Expected behavior
I would like one of the following:
`proxies={}` (or explicit None values) to reliably disable all proxies for that request, including environment proxies; or`trust_env `to be accepted as a per-request argument, e.g. `requests.get(url, trust_env=False)`.

Why this matters
Simple scripts and library wrappers cannot easily switch to a Session.

CI / container environments often set `HTTP_PROXY `/ `HTTPS_PROXY `globally.

Some requests need to use the system proxy while others need to bypass it.

Forcing every caller to create and configure a Session adds unnecessary boilerplate.

Recent proxy-related changes, such as stricter proxy URL parsing in 2.32.0+, make this behavior more visible and harder to work around.

Workaround
Currently the only reliable workaround is:

```
session = requests.Session()
session.trust_env = False
response = session.get(url)
```
This works, but it is not convenient and cannot be applied directly to top-level requests.get() / requests.post() calls.

Proposed API
Allow `trust_env `to be passed per request:

```
requests.get(url, trust_env=False)
```
Alternatively, define `proxies={} `as an explicit opt-out from all environment proxies.

issues.title: Discrepancy in status_codes.py: 102 mapped to "early-hints" instead of 103
Drop the versionless `License ::` classifier now that `license` is a valid SPDX expression
issues.body:
> This issue is part of a larger batch of similar-scoped issues we distribute in the context of our internal vulnerability and dependency tracking activities. The batch covers multiple projects, this is only one of them. The goal is to rise awareness and trigger/initiate the change towards clean project metadata in projects we depend on.

## Summary

This project already declares a valid SPDX license id/expression in its packaging metadata (`License: Apache-2.0` in the built METADATA), but the deprecated classifier `License :: OSI Approved :: Apache Software License` is still present. That classifier has no version and [PEP 639](https://peps.python.org/pep-0639/)-aware SBOM tooling like [cyclonedx-bom](https://pypi.org/project/cyclonedx-bom/) can't map it to an SPDX id, so it falls back to emitting the raw classifier text as a free-text license name. This free-text field is just noise and causes downstream tooling to flag this project as non-SPDX-compliant.

## Suggested fix

Remove the redundant `License :: OSI Approved :: Apache Software License` from `classifiers` in the packaging config. No change to the `license` field is needed.

## How to reproduce

```bash
uv tool install cyclonedx-bom
uv venv .venv-repro
uv pip install --python .venv-repro/bin/python requests
cyclonedx-py environment .venv-repro -o sbom.cdx.json
```

... and then check the `.licenses` property of the component. There should only something like:

```json
// This is how it should look like
...
    "license": {
        "acknowledgement": "declared",
        "id": "<VALID SPDX IDENTIFIER>"
    }
...
```

and _not_:

```json
// This is how it should not look like
...
    "license": {
       "acknowledgement": "declared",
       "name": "<CLASSIFIER TAKEN FROM METADATA"
    }
...
```

I'm happy to provide a PR to resolve this timely after approval!

## Summary

get_redirect_target() and resolve_redirects() in sessions.py follow redirects to any URL without validating the target, allowing SSRF to internal IPs/cloud metadata endpoints.

## Vulnerability

Location: src/requests/sessions.py:134

No validation on redirect targets — can redirect to:
- localhost (127.0.0.0/8)
- RFC 1918 networks (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x)
- Cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254)

- Cloud metadata exfiltration
- Access to internal services

## Fix
Add SSRF protection to redirect resolution:
- Validate redirect target host IP
- Block private/loopback/link-local/multicast IPs
- Add optional allow-list for trusted hosts

issues.title: Cookies are not sent when the URL contains credentials
issues.body:
`requests` extracts credentials embedded in a URL and sends them as an
`Authorization` header, but the same URL then matches no cookie in the jar, so
cookies are silently omitted.

## Expected Result

A cookie scoped to `127.0.0.1` is sent for `http://user:pw@127.0.0.1:PORT/`,
just as it is for `http://127.0.0.1:PORT/`. The userinfo component is not part
of the host (RFC 3986 §3.2), and cookie matching is on the host (RFC 6265).

## Actual Result

The `Authorization` header is sent, but `Cookie` is omitted:

```
without credentials  Authorization=None                  Cookie='sid=secret'
with credentials     Authorization='Basic dXNlcjpwdw=='  Cookie=None
```

The credentials are honoured for authentication, so the URL form is clearly
supported, but cookie matching on that same URL fails. No error or warning is
raised.

## Reproduction Steps

Run a local HTTP server that records the `Authorization` and `Cookie` request
headers it receives. Create a `Session` and set a cookie on it scoped to
`domain="127.0.0.1"`, `path="/"`. Issue two GETs against the server: one to
`http://127.0.0.1:PORT/`, and one to `http://user:pw@127.0.0.1:PORT/`. The
first arrives with the `Cookie` header set and no `Authorization`; the second
arrives with `Authorization` set and no `Cookie`.

issues.title: LookupDict does not implement full contract of the dict class
issues.body:
## Problem Description

The `LookupDict` class in `src/requests/structures.py` subclasses `dict` but does not properly implement the full contract of the `dict` class. Specifically:

1. `__getitem__` and `__getattr__` methods read from `self.__dict__` (plain attribute storage) rather than the actual dict storage
2. All inherited `dict` methods (`__setitem__`, `keys()`, `values()`, `items()`, `get()` via the base class, `in`/`__contains__`, etc.) operate on the *actual* dict storage
3. This creates two disconnected stores, leading to inconsistent behavior

## Reproduction

```python
from requests.status_codes import codes
list(codes.keys())        # returns [] — should include e.g. 'ok', 'not_found', ...
codes["my_code"] = 700    # succeeds (writes to dict storage)
codes["my_code"]          # returns None — should return 700 (read comes from __dict__)
```

## Expected Behavior

1. `list(codes.keys())` should reflect the actual status-code attributes set by `status_codes.py`'s `_init()`
2. `codes["ok"]` (dict-style) and `codes.ok` (attribute-style) should return the same value and stay consistent after either form of assignment
3. Unknown keys should still return `None` via `__getitem__`/`.get()` rather than raising `KeyError` (this is an intentional deviation from plain `dict`)

## Root Cause

In `src/requests/structures.py`, `LookupDict.__getitem__` returns `self.__dict__.get(key, None)` instead of using the dict's own storage.

## Impact

This inconsistency breaks the expected behavior of dict-like objects and prevents users from accessing status codes through standard dict methods.

## Fix

The fix should ensure that `__getitem__` and `__getattr__` methods synchronize with the actual dict storage, maintaining consistency between attribute and dictionary access patterns.

issues.title: raise FileNotFoundError for missing TLS material
issues.body:
Would you accept a PR which changes the existing OSError for missing TLS material to FileNotFoundError?

e.g.:

```
            if conn.cert_file and not os.path.exists(conn.cert_file):
                raise OSError(
                    f"Could not find the TLS certificate file, "
                    f"invalid path: {conn.cert_file}"
                )
```

becomes something like:

```
            if conn.cert_file and not os.path.exists(conn.cert_file):
                from errno import ENOENT
                raise FileNotFoundError(
                    ENOENT,
                    "Could not find the TLS certificate file, invalid path",
                    str(conn.cert_file)
                )
```

Our use case is that there are temporary conditions where the files don't exist and it'd be nicer to handle FileNotFoundError specifically and be able to compare the .filename attribute rather than the more general OSError and test str(excp).endswith(...).  As FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError existing try/excepts continue to work but it would change the string representation:

```
>>> str(OSError("Could not find the TLS certificate file, invalid path: filename"))

```

Any Sphinx project that documents a subclass of `requests.Session` via `:inherited-members:` (or `automodapi`, etc.) now emits this warning. Projects building docs with `-W` / `fail_on_warning: true` (e.g. the Read the Docs default for many projects) fail outright.

## Expected Result

`sphinx-build` renders `Session.get`'s docstring without docutils warnings, as was the case in v2.33.x.

## Actual Result

```
.../mymodule.py:docstring of requests.sessions.Session.get:5: WARNING: Field list ends without a blank line; unexpected unindent. [docutils]
```

```bash

from requests import Session

class MySession(Session):

issues.title: typing.get_type_hints() fails on Response, PreparedRequest, and Request after 2.34.0
issues.body:
When preparing an update to 2.34.2 in Fedora Linux, I've found what I think is a bug in requests.

Since 2.34.0, calling typing.get_type_hints() on any of the three public model classes — or on any subclass of them — raises a NameError at runtime. The minimal reproducer is:

```python
import typing
from requests import Response
typing.get_type_hints(Response)
# NameError: name 'RequestsCookieJar' is not defined
```

The same failure occurs for Request and PreparedRequest.

The 2.34.0 inline typing work introduced three things to models.py simultaneously that interact badly:

1. from `__future__` import annotations (PEP 563) — all annotations are now stored as strings instead of being evaluated eagerly.
2. Class-level annotations on the model classes that reference RequestsCookieJar, CookieJar, and HTTPAdapter:
  - Request.cookies: RequestsCookieJar | CookieJar | dict[str, str] | None
  - PreparedRequest._cookies: RequestsCookieJar | CookieJar | None
  - Response.cookies: RequestsCookieJar
  - Response.connection: HTTPAdapter
3. All three of those names (RequestsCookieJar, CookieJar, HTTPAdapter) are imported only inside if TYPE_CHECKING: — so they are absent from the module's runtime namespace.

When typing.get_type_hints() is called on any of these classes, it evaluates the stored annotation strings in requests.models's runtime globals. The names are not there, so a NameError is raised.

Note that sessions.py gets this right: it imports RequestsCookieJar unconditionally (not under TYPE_CHECKING), so get_type_hints(Session) works correctly. models.py needs to do the same.

Any library that subclasses Response, PreparedRequest, or Request and uses a tool that calls get_type_hints() — such as attrs.resolve_types() (used by cattrs for serialization) — is broken. A confirmed real-world case is requests-cache + requests-ratelimiter: caching any response fails with the NameError because cattrs calls resolve_types(CachedResponse) when building the unstructuring function for a class that inherits from Response.

`prepare_body` stream detection regression
issues.body:
<!-- Summary. -->
Requests 2.34.0 changed the stream detection in PreparedRequest.prepare_body() from `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` to `isinstance(data, Iterable)`. This breaks file-like wrappers that expose `__iter__/read/tell/seek` via `__getattr__ delegation` (e.g. tqdm.wrapattr), because `isinstance(..., Iterable)` only checks the class MRO, not dynamic attribute delegation. As a result, `_body_position` is never recorded and the body cannot be rewound on 307/308 redirects.

Upload completes successfully through the redirect, as it did in 2.33.1.

issues.title: documentation for requests.session.request(verify=...) duplicates requests.request() even where it is different
issues.body:
[Docs currently state](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/#requests.Session.request):

 > Either a boolean, in which case it controls whether we verify the server’s TLS certificate, or a string, in which case it must be a path to a CA bundle to use. Defaults to True.

I suggest rewording both statements, because as they stand they make figuring what went wrong with setting the correct CA bundle way harder than it should be:

1. Passing bool not only controls *whether* the certificate is verified, it [also resets](https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/f43f750ee10addbaa13901c1017631b4d70fd6e3/src/requests/sessions.py#L74) the root store to be verified against.
2. The default for the *method* does **not** behave like True - leaving it unspecified simply defers to the session, as it should.. session in turn may very well have verify=False.
3. (still incomplete because of `os.environ` precedence, but I understand that one is currently #WONTFIX as per https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/3829)

## Documentation appears to state

|                |s.verify=True | s.verify="/S"|s.verify=False|
| -------------- |------------- |------------------- |------------------- |
| s.request(verify=True) | True         | ✅ "/S"              | True               |
| s.request(verify="/r") | "/r"         | "/r"               | "/r"               |
| s.request(verify=False)| False        | False              | False              |
| s.request() # i.e. s.request(verify=None) | True         | ⚠️True               | ⚠️True              |

## Actual Result

|                |s.verify=True | s.verify="/S"|s.verify=False|
| -------------- |------------- |------------------- |------------------- |
| s.request(verify=True) | True         | ⚠️True               | True               |
| s.request(verify="/r") | "/r"         | "/r"               | "/r"               |
| s.request(verify=False)| False        | False              | False              |
| s.request() # i.e. s.request(verify=None) | True         | ✅"/S"               | ✅ False              |

## Reproduction Steps

```python
>>> import certifi,requests,ssl,os
>>> certifi.__version__
'2026.04.22'
>>> certifi.where()
'/inaccessible/path'
>>> requests.__version__
'2.33.1'
>>> session = requests.session()
>>> session.verify = ssl.get_default_verify_paths().capath
>>> os.path.isdir(session.verify)
True
>>> session.request(url="https://example.com", method="HEAD")
<Response [200]>
>>> session.request(url="https://example.com", method="HEAD", verify=True)
Traceback (most recent call last):
[..]
  File "/home/user/lib/python3.10/site-packages/requests/adapters.py", line 304, in cert_verify
    raise OSError(
OSError: Could not find a suitable TLS CA certificate bundle, invalid path: /inaccessible/path
```

This result means that libraries that opt to use the supposedly-default parameter value of True are doing something meaningfully different from those that use the actual-default parameter of None (typically: by not mentioning the parameter).

issues.title: Tweak urllib3 version checker
issues.body:
Hello,

Tiny corner case issue: building urllib3 on my side, I append a marker in the version string to distinguish theses builds, eg.: 2.6.3.build1

Would you consider a small change in requests and split the version string the same way it is done for chardet or charset normalizer ? It would prevent the check from failing on the `major, minor, patch = urllib3_version` line.

```diff
diff --git a/src/requests/__init__.py b/src/requests/__init__.py
@@ -56,7 +56,7 @@ except ImportError:
 
 
 def check_compatibility(urllib3_version, chardet_version, charset_normalizer_version):
-    urllib3_version = urllib3_version.split(".")
+    urllib3_version = urllib3_version.split(".")[:3]
     assert urllib3_version != ["dev"]  # Verify urllib3 isn't installed from git.
 
     # Sometimes, urllib3 only reports its version as 16.1.
```

issues.title: [Docs] Sidebar is hidden in mobile layout
issues.body:
## Problem Description

Theoretically, for documentation using the [alabaster](https://github.com/sphinx-doc/alabaster) theme, the sidebar content should appear at either the **very top** or the **very bottom** in a mobile layout. For example:

- https://alabaster.readthedocs.io/
- https://docs.kernel.org/
- https://www.writethedocs.org/

However, I noticed that the current Requests documentation fails to display sidebar content in its mobile layout.

Based on a preliminary investigation, this issue seems to be caused by modifications to `sphinxsidebar` within the current `custom.css`:

https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/4b0b1a3e9f2fc21b9dcd8b906f2ff02645aa697e/docs/_static/custom.css#L9-L13

The simplest fix is to delete the following line:

```
  div.sphinxsidebar {display: none;}
```

issues.body:
## Summary

We ran [HefestoAI](https://github.com/artvepa80/Agents-Hefesto) (deterministic static analysis, no AI/LLM) against Requests (48 files). The codebase is remarkably clean — only one finding in core code worth noting.

## Finding

### Session lifecycle — `requests/adapters.py:645`

`urlopen()` return value assigned to `resp` without context manager or explicit `.close()`. Potential connection leak if the response is not fully consumed.

This is a minor finding — urllib3's connection pooling likely handles cleanup. Noted for completeness.

## What we didn't find

For the most downloaded Python package in history, this is worth saying: Requests is exceptionally well-maintained. Our full scan at severity LOW produced only code style findings (complexity, function length) beyond this single reliability observation. Zero security findings in core code.

## Reproduction

```bash
pip install hefesto-ai
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/psf/requests.git
hefesto analyze requests/ --severity LOW
```

## About

[HefestoAI](https://github.com/artvepa80/Agents-Hefesto) is an open-source (MIT) deterministic code quality and security analyzer. Sometimes the most useful finding is confirmation that a codebase is clean.

issues.title: Localization of The Requests Documentation
issues.body:
## Announcement

Hello Requests Community,

I am the author of the @localizethedocs organization. And I’m glad to announce that the 🎉 **requests-docs-l10n** 🎉 project is published now:

- 🚀 **Preview:** [requests-docs-l10n](https://projects.localizethedocs.org/requests-docs-l10n)
- 🌐 **Crowdin:** [requests-docs-l10n](https://localizethedocs.crowdin.com/requests-docs-l10n)
- 🐙 **GitHub:** [requests-docs-l10n](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n)

The goal of this project is to translate The Requests Documentation into multiple languages. Translations are contributed via the Crowdin platform, automatically synchronized with the GitHub repository, and can be previewed on GitHub Pages.

## How to Contribute Translations?

To contribute the translations to the project, just follow the following steps:

1. Create an account on [Crowdin Enterprise](https://localizethedocs.crowdin.com/u/signup) if you don't have one.
2. Log in and go the [requests-docs-l10n](https://localizethedocs.crowdin.com/requests-docs-l10n) project.
3. Choose the language you would like to contribute.

If translators want to translate a language that is not yet supported, they just need to open a new [issue](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/issues/new?template=language_request.yml) to request the new language. Once the requested language is added, they can begin translating.

## How to Keep Content Up-to-date?

An FAQ that is sure to come up in the Requests community is: ***How to keep translations up-to-date?***

First and foremost, in my opinion, the focus should be on how to keep the **"Translatable Content (`msgid`)**" up-to-date, rather than the **"Translations (`msgstr`)**". I will focus on the most critical part of the whole infrastructure here.

In short, the [ci-sphinx-update-pot.yml](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci-sphinx-update-pot.yml) workflow will be executed weekly to check the upstream project for any required updates to the document content, which in turn triggers the update of the `.pot` files. If an update is needed, a Pull Request (PR) is automatically created to merge into the `l10n` branch. For example:

- https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/pull/2
- https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/pull/3

Once those PRs are merged, the [ci-gettext-update-po.yml](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci-gettext-update-po.yml) workflow will be triggered to merge the updated content from the `.pot` files into the `.po` files for each language. This is essentially how it keeps the "Translatable Content" up-to-date.

Therefore, the core responsibility of the code maintainers, besides ensuring the stable operation of the scripts and workflows, is to regularly _**check whether there are any pending PRs that need to be merged**_.

## How to Reuse Translations?

If the upstream project or anyone wants to reuse the translated `.po` files prepared by the `requests-docs-l10n` project, they can clone the `.po` files from the `po/${VERSION}` branch by using the following command:

```bash
git clone --depth=1 --branch=po/${VERSION} https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n.git docs/locale
```

Those `po/${VERSION}` branches are created to facilitate reusage by the upstream project. For instance, the `zh_TW` documentation for the `latest` version can be generated using the commands below:

```bash
BRANCH=main
VERSION=latest
LANGUAGE=zh_TW
BUILDER=html

# Prepare the repository and environment
git clone --branch=${BRANCH} https://github.com/psf/requests.git requests-docs
cd requests-docs
conda create --prefix ./.conda --yes
conda activate ./.conda
conda install python=3.13 -c conda-forge -c nodefaults --yes
export PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1
pip install . -r docs/requirements.txt

# Clone the .po files to the 'locale' directory
git clone --branch=po/${VERSION} --depth=1 https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n.git docs/locale

# Build the documentation
sphinx-build \
    -b ${BUILDER} \
    -D language=${LANGUAGE} \
    -D locale_dirs=locale \
    -D gettext_compact=0 \
    -D gettext_additional_targets=index,literal-block,raw \
    docs \
    docs/_build/${LANGUAGE}

# Preview the documentation
firefox docs/_build/${LANGUAGE}/index.html
```

## Related Discussions

There were issues and PRs related to documentation translations:

- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/3033
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/624
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/5902
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/5518
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/2750
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/5679
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/3221
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/2744
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/6142
- https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/1330
- https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/2746
- https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/2751
- https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/6144

And the @requests community **once** actively maintained documentation translations through the "source translation" method:

- Chinese: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-cn
- Japanese: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-jp
- German: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-de
- French: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-fr
- Polish: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-pl
- Portuguese: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-pt
- Dutch: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-nl
- Bulgarian: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-bg
- Arabic: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-ar
- Danish: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-da
- Italian: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-it

However, these efforts were eventually abandoned and became unmaintainable for various reasons. Notably, issue #3033 suggested migrating documentation translations to a TMS platform. Therefore, I believe that the `requests-docs-l10n` project should be able to serve this purpose.

issues.title: [Docs] No clickable button in other pages can return back to the Home page
issues.body: ## Problem Description When visiting the [Quickstart](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/quickstart/) page of the Requests documentation, there is currently no clickable button to return to the [Home](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) page. This could be resolved if other pages (including Quickstart) featured a logo at the top of the left sidebar that links back to the home page, consistent with the Home page itself. The cause of this behavior seems to be as follows: First, in the `html_sidebars` configuration within `conf.py`, the top sidebar template is set to `sidebarintro.html` only for the `index` page. For all other pages, the top template is set to `sidebarlogo.html`: https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/ef439eb779c1eba7cbdeeeb302b11e1e061b4b7d/docs/conf.py#L174-L184 Currently, the hyperlinked logo is only implemented in `sidebarintro.html`: https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/ef439eb779c1eba7cbdeeeb302b11e1e061b4b7d/docs/_templates/sidebarintro.html#L1-L5

issues.title: `check_header_validity` does not reject null bytes and ASCII control characters in header names and values
issues.body:
**Summary:**
`check_header_validity` in `requests/utils.py` silently accepts null bytes (`\x00`) and other ASCII control characters (`\x01`–`\x1f`, `\x7f`) in both header names and values. RFC 7230 Section 3.2.6 forbids these characters in header fields. Only `\r` and `\n` are currently caught.


**Expected Result:**
`check_header_validity` should raise `InvalidHeader` for any header name or value containing null bytes or ASCII control characters, consistent with how `\r` and `\n` are already handled.


**Actual Result:**
```python
from requests.utils import check_header_validity
check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'val\x00ue'))   # no error raised
check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'val\x01ue'))   # no error raised
check_header_validity(('X-Test\x00', 'value'))   # no error raised
```


**Reproduction Steps:**
```python
from requests.utils import check_header_validity
from requests.exceptions import InvalidHeader

# All of these should raise InvalidHeader but do not:
check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'val\x00ue'))
check_header_validity(('X-Test', '\x01value'))
check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'value\x7f'))
check_header_validity(('X-Test\x00', 'value'))

# These correctly raise InvalidHeader:
# check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'val\nue'))   # blocked
# check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'val\rue'))   # blocked
```


**System Information:**
```bash
$ python -m requests.help
```

2.32.2 (2024-05-21)
-------------------

**Deprecations**
- To provide a more stable migration for custom HTTPAdapters impacted
  by the CVE changes in 2.32.0, we've renamed `_get_connection` to
  a new public API, `get_connection_with_tls_context`. Existing custom
  HTTPAdapters will need to migrate their code to use this new API.
  `get_connection` is considered deprecated in all versions of Requests>=2.32.0.

  A minimal (2-line) example has been provided in the linked PR to ease
  migration, but we strongly urge users to evaluate if their custom adapter
  is subject to the same issue described in CVE-2024-35195. (#6710)

releases.name: v2.32.0
releases.body:
2.32.0 (2024-05-20)
-------------------
## 🐍 PYCON US 2024 EDITION 🐍 

**Security**
- Fixed an issue where setting `verify=False` on the first request from a
  Session will cause subsequent requests to the _same origin_ to also ignore
  cert verification, regardless of the value of `verify`.
  (https://github.com/psf/requests/security/advisories/GHSA-9wx4-h78v-vm56)

**Improvements**
- `verify=True` now reuses a global SSLContext which should improve
  request time variance between first and subsequent requests. It should
  also minimize certificate load time on Windows systems when using a Python
  version built with OpenSSL 3.x. (#6667)
- Requests now supports optional use of character detection
  (`chardet` or `charset_normalizer`) when repackaged or vendored.
  This enables `pip` and other projects to minimize their vendoring
  surface area. The `Response.text()` and `apparent_encoding` APIs
  will default to `utf-8` if neither library is present. (#6702)

**Bugfixes**
- Fixed bug in length detection where emoji length was incorrectly
  calculated in the request content-length. (#6589)
- Fixed deserialization bug in JSONDecodeError. (#6629)
- Fixed bug where an extra leading `/` (path separator) could lead
  urllib3 to unnecessarily reparse the request URI. (#6644)

**Deprecations**

- Requests has officially added support for CPython 3.12 (#6503)
- Requests has officially added support for PyPy 3.9 and 3.10 (#6641)
- Requests has officially dropped support for CPython 3.7 (#6642)
- Requests has officially dropped support for PyPy 3.7 and 3.8 (#6641)

**Documentation**
- Various typo fixes and doc improvements.

**Packaging**
- Requests has started adopting some modern packaging practices.
  The source files for the projects (formerly `requests`) is now located
  in `src/requests` in the Requests sdist. (#6506)
- Starting in Requests 2.33.0, Requests will migrate to a PEP 517 build system
  using `hatchling`. This should not impact the average user, but extremely old
  versions of packaging utilities may have issues with the new packaging format.

releases.name: v2.31.0
releases.body:
2.31.0 (2023-05-22)
-------------------

**Security**
- Versions of Requests between v2.3.0 and v2.30.0 are vulnerable to potential
  forwarding of `Proxy-Authorization` headers to destination servers when
  following HTTPS redirects.

  When proxies are defined with user info (https://user:pass@proxy:8080), Requests
  will construct a `Proxy-Authorization` header that is attached to the request to
  authenticate with the proxy.

  In cases where Requests receives a redirect response, it previously reattached
  the `Proxy-Authorization` header incorrectly, resulting in the value being
  sent through the tunneled connection to the destination server. Users who rely on
  defining their proxy credentials in the URL are *strongly* encouraged to upgrade
  to Requests 2.31.0+ to prevent unintentional leakage and rotate their proxy
  credentials once the change has been fully deployed.

  Users who do not use a proxy or do not supply their proxy credentials through
  the user information portion of their proxy URL are not subject to this
  vulnerability.

  Full details can be read in our [Github Security Advisory](https://github.com/psf/requests/security/advisories/GHSA-j8r2-6x86-q33q)
  and [CVE-2023-32681](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-32681).

releases.name: v2.27.0
releases.body:
2.27.0 (2022-01-03)
-------------------

**Improvements**

- Officially added support for Python 3.10. (#5928)

- Added a `requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError` to unify JSON exceptions between
  Python 2 and 3. This gets raised in the `response.json()` method, and is
  backwards compatible as it inherits from previously thrown exceptions.
  Can be caught from `requests.exceptions.RequestException` as well. (#5856)

- Improved error text for misnamed `InvalidSchema` and `MissingSchema`
  exceptions. This is a temporary fix until exceptions can be renamed
  (Schema->Scheme). (#6017)

- Improved proxy parsing for proxy URLs missing a scheme. This will address
  recent changes to `urlparse` in Python 3.9+. (#5917)

**Bugfixes**

- Fixed defect in `extract_zipped_paths` which could result in an infinite loop
  for some paths. (#5851)

- Fixed handling for `AttributeError` when calculating length of files obtained
  by `Tarfile.extractfile()`. (#5239)

- Fixed urllib3 exception leak, wrapping `urllib3.exceptions.InvalidHeader` with
  `requests.exceptions.InvalidHeader`. (#5914)

- Fixed bug where two Host headers were sent for chunked requests. (#5391)

- Fixed regression in Requests 2.26.0 where `Proxy-Authorization` was
  incorrectly stripped from all requests sent with `Session.send`. (#5924)

- Fixed performance regression in 2.26.0 for hosts with a large number of
  proxies available in the environment. (#5924)

- Fixed idna exception leak, wrapping `UnicodeError` with
  `requests.exceptions.InvalidURL` for URLs with a leading dot (.) in the
  domain. (#5414)

**Deprecations**

- Requests support for Python 2.7 and 3.6 will be ending in 2022. While we
  don't have exact dates, Requests 2.27.x is likely to be the last release
  series providing support.
